Last week, I had the pleasure of listening and learning from senior software engineers, solutions architects, and recruitment leaders from Amazon Web Services (AWS) at the AWS AI Innovation Showcase."
""
"Alongside great food, free pens and a full day of sessions, we had the chance to hear directly from AWS experts about the future of AI and network with the keynote speakers afterwards."
""
"One of the talks that stood out to me was from David Bounds, who walked us through the history of generative AI. From early word to vector representations, to the Attention Is All You Need paper all the way to the context-driven architectures behind today’s models like GPT. It was a great refresher and highlighted that at AWS not only should you be thinking about what to innovate for the future with AI but it's crucial to know how we got here as well."
""
"I also really enjoyed Yuri Makarov session on robotics at AWS. He explained how AWS is heavily investing in robotic systems and even showed a very awesome demo of a humanoid robot performing a backflip inside one of Amazon’s warehouses. He also discussed some of the major technical challenges such as the resource demands of having a robot use a VLM to navigate a space while simultaneously maintaining a digital twin that updates in real time based on the robot’s sensor feedback. Even with all of this, the digital twin can still be inaccurate. Whilst AWS has the resources to support this for individual robots or even a few hundred, scaling it efficiently to full operational levels remains one of the challenges."
""
"Overall, the event was incredibly inspiring and gave me a deeper appreciation for AWS in particular with regards to AI and robotics. I definitely feel like I need to research and learn a lot more now given the sheer range of topics and cool demos that were shown."
""
"I’d also like to thank Matthew Parker for the warm introduction and for answering several of my questions, and Martin Angelovski for the engaging conversation about quantum computing, AWS’s work in this field, and how technologies like AWS Trainium fit into the broader research landscape at AWS."
""

Last week I attended a 2 hour master class  about AWS by an industry expert "
""
"Here’s everything I learnt."
""
"AMAZON’S UNIQUE APPROACH "
""
"Around the early 2000s Amazon took a unique approach in comparison to Google and Microsoft by:"
""
"-Building the Nitro system ( a custom hardware and software platform that powered it’s cloud instances efficiently and securely)"
""
"-Introducing the pay as you go model for cloud services "
""
"-Building its own custom  databases from scratch which could ensure high availability and again high efficiency "
""
"This all built a strong ecosystem that helped AWS dominate the cloud market."
""
"HOW AMAZON STAYED AHEAD OF COMPETITION"
""
"I also learnt how in lockdown the surge in number of users on the internet was immense, more than 300 million new users, and with this came the rise in platforms like TikTok and Netflix."
""
"What did this mean? It meant data traffic was increasing as well. "
""
"A great analogy for this given by the guest speaker was like driving hundreds of lorries on a residential road , it’s not built for it and it’s going to cause delays and traffic. "
""
"Something that Google and Microsoft weren’t as prepared for as AWS. AWS  had a larger more distributed global network of private data centres that were a lot easier to scale to meet demand. This was all thought out in advance by Amazon around 2010. They predicted this surge in usage eventually and so invested heavily in their private networks."
""
"Why should this matter? If you can’t deal with high amounts of data traffic you’re going to experience delays and delays cost money, a lot of money. Amazon found every 0.1 second of latency cost 1% of all their sales which at the time would’ve cost 342 million dollars 🤯."
""
""
"In conclusion, Amazon stayed ahead of its competition and remained dominant in the cloud market through innovation and deep understanding of trends."
""

ZKP"
""
"Explaining zero knowledge proofs(something that I found quite unique and interesting) on a basic level."
""
"The example I’ve found the easiest to understand ZKP is as follows:"
""
"-Consider you have two people person A and person B where person B is colour blind."
""
"-Person B has two cards, one red and one green, which are identical in all aspects apart from colour."
""
"-Person A wants to prove to person B that both are different (as B thinks otherwise being colour blind)"
""
"Now in order for A to prove it B puts the red card in one hand and the green in the other and shows it to A. B now shuffles the cards behind his back keeping in mind what card was originally in his left and right hand respectively. Now B holds out both cards again and if the arrangement changes(let’s say red was originally in the right hand and green in the other and now it’s vice versa ) person A will know as the colours have swapped hands. If not then A will also know as by seeing the colours he will know they have not changed position. In order to ensure this is not a fluke B will repeat this process multiple times."
""
"In conclusion given A answers correctly for a large amount of times A proves to B there is a difference DESPITE person B not being able to tell which card is which colour and so proving to B there is a difference between them without B knowing the difference. This relates to cybersecurity as a big company may want for example some data without having to reveal the data itself or for example if someone wants to prove they know a password to a safe without saying what the password is. Essentially it is a way to prove something to someone whilst also giving no knowledge to the person about what it is that you’ve done to prove it, hence the name ‘zero knowledge’ proof. #cybersecurity #data #tech #security #datasecurity #encryption
